source.version: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Working Papers No. 16/WP/2026 (ISSN 1827-3580), with the online appendix bound in; the online appendix is dated February 2026 (PDF p. 30). Main text carries no date of its own.
source.title_on_document: Human-AI Interaction in Creative Tasks: an Experimental Investigation

supplement.holds: Appendix A: lab and survey instructions (English translation); Appendix B: construction and Python code for Idea request, Idea request index, Similarity; Appendix C Table 1: mediation SEMs with Zhu and Zou (2026) AI-first and User-first keywords. All creativity-score statistics used here (Tables 1, 2, 5) are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: Lab experiment at VERALabEx (Ca' Foscari, Venice) with 360 mainly student participants in a 2 x 3 between-subjects design: access to ChatGPT-4.2 embedded in the oTree interface (AI vs. No AI) crossed with three incentive schemes (piece rate, tournament, lottery). Each participant wrote one short creative composition (about 150 words, about 15 minutes) answering 'If you had the talent to create something simply with your thoughts, what would you create?'. Four blind Italian-speaking Prolific raters scored each text for creativity, and the main outcome is the mean of the four scores.

studies.label: Lab experiment, 2 x 3 (AI access x incentive scheme), creative composition

assignment.what_was_assigned: One of six treatment cells: AI access (ChatGPT-4.2 assistant in the interface) or no AI, crossed with tournament, piece-rate, or lottery incentive scheme
assignment.quote: The experiment was implemented in oTree (Chen et al., 2016). Participants were randomly assigned to treatments and completed comprehension questions before the task.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 5), Section 2.1 Experimental Procedures; 2 x 3 between-subjects design at PDF p. 6 (printed p. 3), Section 2.1

arms.name: T&AI
arms.description: Tournament incentive (top of a gender-balanced group of four earns 2.4 euros per point), with ChatGPT access

arms.name: PR&AI
arms.description: Piece rate (0.6 euros times average score), with ChatGPT access

arms.name: L&AI
arms.description: Lottery (one in four receives 15 euros regardless of performance), with ChatGPT access

participants.exclusions: None reported. The paper says the experiment was conducted with 360 participants who were randomly assigned to treatments; Table 1 cell counts (52+47+49+88+62+62) sum to 360 and Tables 2 and 5 use 360 observations (148 no-AI, 212 AI). The paper gives no separate count at assignment, so 360 randomized rests on the statement that all 360 participants were randomly assigned.
participants.who: Participants at VERALabEx, primarily students in economics-related programs; Italian as first language required
participants.quote: The experiment was conducted at VERALabEx (Ca' Foscari University of Venice) with 360 participants, primarily students in economics-related programs. Eligibility required Italian as a first language.
participants.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 5), Section 2.1 Experimental Procedures; cell counts PDF p. 14 (printed p. 11), Table 1, row Obs.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4.2 (as named by the paper), via API embedded in the oTree interface
ai_tool.how_used: Participants in AI cells could send any number of free-form queries to an embedded ChatGPT box during the writing task, with no restrictions; access ended when they submitted the composition. Share who sent at least one query: 0.818 (T&AI), 0.677 (PR&AI), 0.790 (L&AI) (Table 1).

task.description: Short creative composition answering 'If you had the talent to create something simply with your thoughts, what would you create?' (Charness and Grieco, 2019); open task, suggested length about 150 words
task.duration: Suggested no more than 15 minutes (indicative only); sessions lasted about 50 minutes

outcomes.name: Average creativity score (mean of four Prolific raters' scores of the composition)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Four independent Italian-speaking Prolific raters per text, each rater scoring four randomly assigned texts, blind to AI and incentive condition; position counterbalanced. Main text says a 1 to 10 scale (PDF p. 9); the rater instructions say 'from 0 to 10' (PDF p. 34, appendix p. 5). Outcome is the mean of the four ratings per text. Participant payment depended on this score in PR and T cells.

contrasts.reported: Table 5 col (1), OLS with Tournament and Piece Rate dummies: AI 0.398** (robust SE 0.139); constant 5.681***; N = 360. Table 2 col (1), OLS controlling for number of characters, male, DAT score, DAT score squared: AI 0.299* (0.131); N = 360.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 23 (printed p. 20), Table 5 col (1); PDF p. 16 (printed p. 13), Table 2 col (1)

contrasts.reported: Average score T&AI 6.281 (SD 1.363, n = 88) vs T 5.615 (SD 1.317, n = 52); no test reported for this cell contrast
Average score PR&AI 6.000 (SD 1.363, n = 62) vs PR 5.681 (SD 1.089, n = 47); no test reported for this cell contrast
Average score L&AI 5.972 (SD 1.329, n = 62) vs L 5.816 (SD 1.311, n = 49); no test reported for this cell contrast

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI-access participants split by self-selected use: AI (use) = sent at least one query; AI (no use) = sent none
contrasts.reported: Table 2 col (2), OLS with characters, male, DAT, DAT squared: AI (use) 0.411** (0.138); AI (no use) -0.082 (0.231); N = 360. Split on post-assignment behavior, so not a randomized contrast.

outcomes.name: Number of characters in the composition
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mechanical length count (characters) of the final text; not a creativity scoring model. The codebook has no measure code for a length count, so automated_score is the nearest code.

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 23 (printed p. 20), Table 5 col (2); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 11), Table 1

outcomes.name: Divergent Association Task (DAT) score, post-experiment questionnaire
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DAT (Olson et al., 2021): average semantic distance (0 to 100) between the words the participant lists. Completed in the post-experimental questionnaire, after the writing task, when ChatGPT access had ended. The paper treats it as a measure of baseline creative potential and a control, not as a treatment outcome, but Table 5 col (3) regresses it on AI access.
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the writing task and later stages

contrasts.locator: PDF p. 23 (printed p. 20), Table 5 col (3); PDF p. 14 (printed p. 11), Table 1

company_involvement.description: Funded by PRIN 2022 project GENS (N. 20229RB8HY); no company involvement stated. ChatGPT accessed via API; Claude 4.6 Sonnet used to classify queries.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 3, funding footnote; PDF p. 27 (printed p. 24), AI declaration

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly assigned to ChatGPT access or no AI (crossed with incentive schemes) in a between-subjects lab design (PDF p. 8); 360 people analyzed, 212 AI and 148 no-AI (Table 2, PDF p. 16); creativity of each composition rated by four blind Prolific raters (PDF p. 9).

one_line_finding: In a lab experiment with 360 Italian students, ChatGPT access raised the raters' average creativity score of a short composition by 0.398 points (SE 0.139) on a roughly 10-point scale (Table 5 col 1, PDF p. 23; 0.299, SE 0.131, with controls in Table 2 col 1), with the gain concentrated among participants who actually queried the AI.
open_questions: Unit of assignment: the paper says participants were randomly assigned to treatments, but it also refers to 'sessions conducted under the tournament condition' (PDF p. 8) and the instructions describe 20 people per session, which suggests treatment may have varied by session. Standard errors are robust, not clustered by session.
Arm sizes are unbalanced (T&AI 88 vs. 47 to 62 in other cells, Table 1) and the paper does not explain why.
Rating scale: main text says 1 to 10 (PDF p. 9), rater instructions say 0 to 10 (PDF p. 34).
Table 2 col (1) controls for number of characters, which AI access itself raises (Table 5 col 2), so Table 5 col (1) is the cleaner AI-access contrast.
Whether the DAT score, taken after AI access ended and used by the paper as a baseline covariate, should be coded as an after_ai outcome.
notes: Outcome-level SDs are available only by cell (Table 1); pooled AI vs no-AI means and SDs are not printed. Mediation analyses (Table 3, PDF p. 18; Appendix C Table 1, PDF p. 53) and Table 4 (PDF p. 21) are restricted to the 212 AI-access participants and relate the creativity score to self-selected AI use (Idea request, Similarity, number of queries); they are not randomized contrasts and are not listed as outcomes. Similarity (TF-IDF cosine between the final text and the AI responses) measures reliance on AI, not diversity across people, so it is not coded as an across_people outcome. Table 2 col (3) reports AI -0.163 (0.181) once number of queries and its square enter; cols (4)-(5) split the sample by AI arm. Stage 2 (competition choice) is analyzed in a separate study and is outside this paper. Eligible core paper; no diversity outcome.
